profiles.summary: Bangladesh insists that the health of over a million Rohingya refugees is a global responsibility, not Bangladesh’s burden, and fights to keep the patent flexibilities that protect its generic medicine industry.

priorities.text: Predictable, multi-year international funding for refugee health as a shared global responsibility.
Keep or extend TRIPS patent flexibilities and support compulsory licensing to protect its generics industry.
PABS benefit-sharing and technology transfer for regional manufacturing.
Recognition of climate change as a health threat, and support for the Pandemic Fund.
Continued access to grants and soft loans despite rising income.

redLines.text: No language implying the Rohingya should be integrated or permanently settled in Bangladesh.
No shifting of refugee health costs onto the Bangladeshi budget.
No ‘TRIPS-plus’ intellectual property obligations.
No criticism of Bangladesh’s post-2024 political transition.

interests.text: Hosts over a million Rohingya refugees from Myanmar in Cox’s Bazar. The 2026 UN response plan asks for US$710.5 million, 26% less than 2025. The US cut about US$200 million in early 2025, and at least 11 health centres closed in 18 months, leaving about 300,000 refugees without nearby care.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman presented a five-point plan at the UN General Assembly in September 2026 demanding a roadmap for Rohingya repatriation and ‘predictable funding’.

Is due to graduate from Least Developed Country status on 4 Nov 2026; the BNP government asked the UN to defer it. Graduation would end Bangladesh’s exemption from WTO drug-patent rules, threatening its large generic pharmaceutical export industry and raising medicine prices.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with India, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, China (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Moral appeals combined with concrete requests. Raises the Rohingya crisis in every discussion and works through the OIC and LDC group. Earnest and appealing to conscience: ‘shared responsibility’, ‘burden-sharing’, ‘a crisis not of our making’. Stresses Bangladesh’s generosity in hosting refugees.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.summary: Brazil champions universal public health systems, local production of vaccines and medicines, and a Pandemic Agreement that puts benefit-sharing on an equal footing with pathogen access, positioning itself as the Global South’s bridge-builder.

priorities.text: Conclude the PABS annex within 2026, with ‘equal footing between access and benefit sharing’ and no weakening of the 20% production commitment in Article 12.
Expand local and regional production of vaccines and medicines through technology transfer (the Fiocruz model and the PAHO Revolving Fund for pooled vaccine purchasing).
Promote universal public health systems like the SUS as the answer to collapsing aid, rather than donor-run disease programmes.
Link health to climate justice, hunger and poverty reduction.
Reform global health architecture to give the Global South more voice.

redLines.text: No reopening of equity commitments already agreed in the Pandemic Agreement.
No PABS system where benefits are voluntary or come too late.
No intellectual property language restricting compulsory licensing. Brazil broke the patent on the HIV drug efavirenz in 2007 and is proud of it.
Under Lula, Brazil defends gender equality and sexual and reproductive health language against deletion.
No language condemning Russia by name.

interests.text: Brazil’s Unified Health System (SUS) provides free universal care to over 200 million people and is Lula’s showcase model.
Law 15.471 of 20 July 2026 created a national strategy to produce more vaccines and medicines domestically (Health Economic-Industrial Complex).
Hosted COP30 in Belém (November 2025); its Health Ministry presented the draft Belém Health Action Plan, linking climate and health, in Brasília in July 2025.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with Mexico, South Africa, India, Indonesia, Norway (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Bridge-builder and convenor. Constructive and ambitious on deadlines. Proposes compromise texts and tries to bring Europeans and Africans together, while firmly in the developing-country camp on equity. Warm, values-driven and expansive. Talks about social justice, the SUS, fighting hunger and the climate emergency. Frequently invokes ‘solidarity’ and ‘the right to health’.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.
Election outcome updated 2026-11-27: Lula won the runoff; treat Brazil's commitments as continuing.

profiles.summary: China advocates for equitable global health cooperation that strengthens developing countries’ healthcare capacity, promotes access to medical technology, and respects national sovereignty and non-interference in domestic affairs.

priorities.text: Champion WHO’s ‘central coordinating role’ and multilateralism, presenting China as the responsible power in contrast to US withdrawal.
Reform global health governance so developing countries get more voice and representation.
Press developed countries to ‘fulfil their financial obligations’ and restore aid, while framing China’s own contributions as South-South solidarity rather than donor charity.
Strengthen health systems in developing countries through workforce training, medical technology sharing, and access to essential medicines and vaccines.
In the PABS talks, back legally certain benefit-sharing rules alongside the developing-country camp.
Expand bilateral health cooperation (Africa CDC, BRICS vaccine centre, Chinese medical teams) as an alternative to Western aid.

redLines.text: No participation by Taiwan ‘in any form’: no observer status, no references to Taiwan’s health system or data-sharing.
No new COVID-origins investigations, lab audits or WHO verification on Chinese territory without its consent.
No resolutions that name or condemn Russia.
No international health initiatives it sees as politically motivated or as interfering in internal affairs, including human rights language aimed at Xinjiang or Tibet.
No intellectual property arrangements that restrict developing countries’ access to medical technology, and no dues formula that makes China the top payer without matching influence.

interests.text: Pledged US$500 million to WHO over five years in May 2025, becoming its largest state donor after the US exit. The pledge mixes higher assessed dues, voluntary money and South-South projects; how much has been paid out is unclear.

In Feb 2025 China was one of only two states that opposed the 20% increase in WHO assessed contributions, citing a sluggish global economy. Under the new UN scale its share of dues rises from about 15% to 20%.
WHA79 (May 2026) again refused to invite Taiwan as an observer, the 10th year in a row, with China and Pakistan opposing.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with Russia, India, South Africa, Brazil, DR Congo, Indonesia (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Confident and well resourced. Presents itself as the defender of multilateralism and the Global South, and uses funding as leverage. Prefers consensus language but will not move at all on sovereignty, Taiwan or COVID origins. Often works through the G77 rather than alone. Formal, measured and slogan-like (‘true multilateralism’, ‘a community with a shared future for mankind’, ‘win-win cooperation’). Rarely attacks countries by name, but makes pointed references to ‘certain countries’ that abandon their responsibilities.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.summary: The DRC advocates for equitable access to healthcare through sustained international funding, strengthened domestic healthcare infrastructure, and coordinated disease prevention efforts that respect national sovereignty.

priorities.text: Increased international financial and technical assistance to strengthen healthcare infrastructure, train medical personnel, improve disease surveillance and provide emergency medical supplies.
Fast, flexible emergency money for the Ebola response, through WHO’s contingency fund, the Pandemic Fund and donors, channelled through the government: ‘one plan, one team, one budget’.
Research, development and fair access for Bundibugyo vaccines and treatments, with trials run in the DRC and benefits returned to the DRC.
A strong PABS benefit-sharing system, since samples from the DRC have fed vaccine development before without guaranteed returns.
WHO coordination and international cooperation to contain outbreaks before they cross borders, including protection for health workers and humanitarian access in conflict zones.

redLines.text: Preserve national sovereignty and control over domestic healthcare decisions; no parallel aid structures run by NGOs that bypass the Health Ministry.
No discriminatory travel restrictions against Congolese people (such as Saudi Arabia’s Ebola visa ban).
No language implying the government is incapable or corrupt.
No text that treats Rwanda or M23 as neutral actors, or that ignores how the conflict drives the epidemic.
No emergency responses that undermine long-term health system development, and no sharing of samples without benefits returned.

interests.text: Is fighting the largest Ebola outbreak in its history: the Bundibugyo strain, declared on 15 May 2026 in Ituri and declared a global health emergency (PHEIC) by WHO on 17 May. By mid-October 2026 there were roughly 9,000 confirmed cases and 4,400 deaths across seven provinces. There is no licensed vaccine or treatment for this strain.
Has handled 16 earlier Ebola outbreaks and presents itself as the world’s most experienced Ebola responder.
Before the cuts, USAID gave the DRC over US$1 billion a year (2023), mostly for health and humanitarian work. The US funded over 70% of humanitarian action in the country in 2024.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Indonesia, China, France (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Appeals for solidarity from the position of a country on the front line of a global emergency. Defensive about sovereignty and quick to push back on criticism of its government. Works through the Africa Group and the Group for Equity. Urgent and emotional, grounded in the human cost of the outbreak and in its long experience fighting Ebola. Formal diplomatic French-influenced phrasing (‘Honourable Chair’, ‘no country can contain emerging epidemics alone’).
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.summary: France speaks grandly of multilateralism, One Health and reforming the global health architecture, and defends reproductive rights as part of its ‘feminist diplomacy’, while making the deepest aid cuts in the G7.

priorities.text: Reform of the ‘global health architecture’ led from Europe.
A ‘One Health’ approach linking human, animal and environmental health.
Finalise the Pandemic Agreement and PABS annex.
Champion multilateralism against US unilateralism.
Support Africa CDC and local African production, especially in francophone Africa.
Defend sexual and reproductive health and rights and gender equality.

redLines.text: No rollback of sexual and reproductive health or gender language.
No PABS terms that undermine the European pharmaceutical base or intellectual property.
No new financial commitments that parliament will not pass.

interests.text: The 2026 budget, forced through without a parliamentary vote, cut aid by about €800 million (−18%). Aid in 2025 was €12.9 billion, 0.42% of national income, the lowest since 2017. The 2027 draft budget cuts it again; aid credits have roughly halved in three years.
Cut its Global Fund pledge for 2026–28 by 58% and Unitaid by 22%.
President Macron hosted the One Health Summit in Lyon in April 2026, where NGOs protested the ‘amputation’ of France’s Global Fund contribution. France also hosts the WHO Academy in Lyon.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with Germany, Norway, United Kingdom, DR Congo, Brazil (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Ambitious and visionary in speeches, careful in the details. Proposes summits, initiatives and frameworks, and coordinates with the EU while cultivating francophone Africa. Grand and philosophical, sometimes in French. Talks about ‘multilateralism’, ‘solidarity’, ‘architecture’, ‘One Health’ and European leadership.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.summary: Germany wants a lean, efficient WHO focused on its core mandate and a pathogen-sharing system that keeps pharmaceutical research attractive, while it cuts development aid to pay for defence and calls itself WHO’s most reliable funder.

priorities.text: A ‘strong WHO that focuses on its core competencies’: norms and standards, health security and coordination.
WHO reform and efficiency in return for continued funding.
Prioritise antimicrobial resistance and health security.
A PABS system that works for industry, with pathogens kept out of the Nagoya biodiversity protocol’s rules.
Act as a bridge-builder within the EU.

redLines.text: No mandatory, standardised benefit-sharing contracts that ‘stifle R&D’.
No weakening of intellectual property or TRIPS protections.
No open-ended new spending commitments.
No retreat on gender equality and sexual and reproductive health language.

interests.text: After the US exit, Germany says it is WHO’s largest financial contributor. At WHA79 it pledged an extra €25 million, mainly for cross-border outbreaks.

The development ministry’s core budget has fallen from €12.4 billion (2021) to €9.9 billion (2026), and the 2027 plan cuts it by a further 5.8%. The government dropped the 0.7% aid target and ended bilateral health cooperation with partner countries.
Funding for the WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence in Berlin was halved from about €30m a year to €15m, with only one year committed (Health Policy Watch, 8 Jan 2026).

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with France, United Kingdom, Japan, Norway, Republic of Korea (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Technocratic, legalistic and ‘constructive’. Negotiates through EU coordination, defends industry interests in detailed text, and uses its funding role to demand reform. Precise, sober and rule-focused: ‘efficiency’, ‘core mandate’, ‘accountability’, ‘sustainable financing’. Avoids grand rhetoric.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.summary: India demands a fair, legally binding pandemic system that guarantees the Global South access to vaccines, medicines and technology, protects generic manufacturing, and positions India as the world’s affordable pharmacy without accepting outside intrusion into its sovereignty.

priorities.text: PABS: standardised, legally binding contracts at the point of pathogen access, with digital traceability of samples and sequence data.
Equitable access to vaccines, tests and treatments through technology transfer and regional manufacturing, with India as a central hub.
Protect generic medicine production and TRIPS flexibilities, including compulsory licensing.
Bring traditional medicine (Ayush) into WHO frameworks for primary health care and universal health coverage.
Promote India’s digital public health infrastructure (such as the CoWIN vaccination platform and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission) as a global public good.

redLines.text: No language that restricts TRIPS flexibilities, compulsory licensing or generic manufacturing.
No intrusive verification, compliance reviews or WHO powers that override national decisions.
No PABS deal that gives pharmaceutical companies free access to pathogens without enforceable benefits for developing countries.
No resolutions naming Russia (abstained on WHA79/11).
No criticism of Indian drug quality that could be used to justify trade barriers against Indian generics.

interests.text: The central health ministry’s 2026–27 budget is about ₹1.02 lakh crore: 1.96% of central government spending and under 0.3% of GDP. The 2017 target of 2.5% of GDP in public health spending (all levels of government) by 2025 was missed.
Voted for the Pandemic Agreement in May 2025. Modi addressed WHA78, promoting the Ayushman Bharat insurance scheme and low-cost public pharmacies as models for the Global South.
Hosts the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre in Jamnagar and co-hosted the 2nd WHO Global Summit on Traditional Medicine in December 2025.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Russia (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Assertive, technical and legalistic. Fights hard over treaty wording on intellectual property and sovereignty, and speaks as the ‘voice of the Global South’. Avoids taking sides on Russia. Cooperates with China on equity but competes with it for leadership of the developing world. Confident, data-heavy and proud of Indian achievements (‘the world’s largest health insurance scheme’, ‘vaccines for 100 countries’). Uses phrases like ‘equity, not charity’ and ‘One Earth, One Health’ (Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam).
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.basis: team research reviewed 2026-10-17 (sources listed); key claims sample-checked 2026-11-27
profiles.summary: Indonesia leads the developing world’s demand for a legally binding pathogen-sharing system with guaranteed benefits, while courting donors and the US as its health minister campaigns to become WHO’s next Director-General.

priorities.text: A legally binding, enforceable PABS annex that starts operating together with the Pandemic Agreement, with nothing left to be decided later.
Real benefit-sharing: about 20% of pandemic products reserved for WHO, annual payments from companies that use the system, and no anonymous users of pathogen data.
Local and regional vaccine and biotech manufacturing (such as the state company Bio Farma) and technology transfer.
A leaner, more ‘useful’ WHO focused on core work and funded partly by development banks, with countries moving from grants to loans to domestic financing.
Keep the door open to the US re-engaging with global health.

redLines.text: No PABS annex that merely repeats Article 12 of the Agreement or contains ‘major loopholes’.
No pathogen sharing without guaranteed benefits.
No delay in making the PABS system operational.

interests.text: Founded and leads the Group for Equity, a coalition of over 30 developing countries in the PABS negotiations, and coordinates with the Africa Group.
In 2007 Indonesia refused to share H5N1 bird flu samples until it was guaranteed access to resulting vaccines, the episode that started the global debate on benefit-sharing.
The Pandemic Fund was launched under Indonesia’s G20 presidency in 2022.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with South Africa, Brazil, India, Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia, DR Congo (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Confident, technocratic bridge-builder. Leads the Group for Equity firmly on PABS, but presents itself as a reasonable partner who can bring North and South together, partly to build support for its Director-General candidate. Crisp and business-like, with memorable metaphors (PABS is ‘the heart of the Pandemic Agreement’). Talks about efficiency, results and financing like a banker.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.basis: team research reviewed 2026-10-17 (sources listed); key claims sample-checked 2026-11-27
profiles.summary: Japan frames everything through universal health coverage and ‘human security’, pushing countries toward self-reliant health financing, while it halves its global health pledges, funds record defence spending and stands firm against China over Taiwan.

priorities.text: Universal health coverage and ‘human security’ as the organising frame for global health.
Move countries toward domestic resource mobilisation and self-reliant health financing.
Health security and emergency preparedness, including through the UHC Knowledge Hub.
A PABS system that preserves incentives for research and development.
Resilient medical supply chains as part of economic security.

redLines.text: No mandatory technology transfer or intellectual property waivers.
No binding financing targets.
No language that legitimises China’s position on Taiwan.

interests.text: FY2026 defence budget is a record ¥9.04 trillion, about 2% of GDP.
Pledged up to ¥81 billion (about US$515 million) to the Global Fund for 2026–28 — about half its previous pledge in dollar terms (about 20% less in yen).
Co-founded the UHC Knowledge Hub with the World Bank and WHO in Tokyo (December 2025), now supporting eight countries. Co-hosted a side event on UHC financing with Nigeria at WHA79.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with Republic of Korea, Germany, United Kingdom, France, Nigeria (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Formal, consensus-oriented and non-confrontational. Works quietly through the G7 and bilateral partnerships, and is careful but firm on China. Polite, understated and repetitive in its framing: ‘universal health coverage’, ‘human security’, ‘self-reliance’, ‘leave no one behind’. Rarely names other countries.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.basis: team research reviewed 2026-10-17 (sources listed); key claims sample-checked 2026-11-27
profiles.summary: Kenya presents itself as Africa’s model of ‘ownership’ and co-financing, the reliable partner that can work with Washington and Geneva at once, while defending the bilateral deals and health-worker exports that critics say undercut African solidarity.

priorities.text: Showcase Kenya’s ‘co-financing and transition’ model and attract investment, including regional headquarters and vaccine manufacturing.
Domestic financing for universal health coverage through the SHA, plus debt relief and fairer international financing.
Stronger Africa CDC, regional manufacturing and pooled procurement.
‘Managed’ health-worker migration that pays back through remittances or training funds, not restrictions.
Data sovereignty language that does not threaten its US agreement.

redLines.text: No text implying that bilateral data and sample-sharing deals undermine the multilateral PABS system.
No restrictions on health-worker mobility; Kenya benefits from remittances.
No criticism of the SHA’s governance.
No binding obligations without flexibility on co-financing.

interests.text: USAID gave Kenya about US$470 million a year in 2020–25, roughly 80% of it for health.
Was the first African country to sign a US ‘America First’ health deal (4 Dec 2025): about US$1.6 billion from the US over five years, with US$850 million of Kenyan co-financing rising each year.

The deal includes sharing of medical records, genomic and pathogen data, and biological samples with the US. Kenya’s High Court froze it in December 2025; the Court of Appeal allowed it to proceed on 9 Oct 2026, but the constitutional case continues.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with United States, Nigeria, South Africa, United Kingdom, Norway (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Polished and business-like. Positions Kenya as a bridge between donors and Africa and between the US and WHO. Avoids open confrontation but defends its own deals firmly. Upbeat, entrepreneurial language: ‘ownership’, ‘self-reliance’, ‘investment, not aid’, ‘government-to-government’. Highlights Kenyan innovation and leadership.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.basis: team research reviewed 2026-10-17 (sources listed); key claims sample-checked 2026-11-27
profiles.summary: The Republic of Korea offers its COVID-19 response expertise and biomanufacturing know-how as a bridge between donors and developing countries, while cutting humanitarian aid in half and funding visible WHO projects that also promote its own bio industry.

priorities.text: Strengthen health security and emergency response, drawing on Korea’s COVID-19 experience (testing, tracing, digital tools).
Build biomanufacturing capacity in developing countries through training and partnerships.
Support WHO reform and efficiency during budget cuts.
Promote digital health.
Act as a bridge between donors and developing countries.

redLines.text: No PABS terms that burden export-oriented Korean vaccine and biologics manufacturers.
No hard financing targets after its aid cuts.
Avoid antagonising either China or the US.

interests.text: The Foreign Ministry's 2025 budget proposal cut its ODA by about 22% (KRW 2.81tn to 2.19tn) and humanitarian aid by about 51% (Korea Herald, 29 Aug 2025).
President Lee ordered a review of whether aid projects serve ‘national prestige and diplomatic goals’, amid a probe into alleged aid-related influence-peddling involving the former first lady.
Funded the JW Lee Strategic Situation Room at WHO headquarters (opened May 2026), named after Lee Jong-wook, the Korean WHO Director-General who died in office in 2006.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with Japan, Germany, Indonesia, United Kingdom (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Low-key, technical and pragmatic. Leads with expertise rather than ideology, avoids open confrontation, and keeps good relations with the US, China and the Global South. Modest and solution-oriented. Shares concrete Korean experience (‘K-quarantine’, digital health, biomanufacturing training) and speaks of ‘bridging’ and ‘partnership’.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.summary: Mexico defends health as a right delivered by a strong public state, backs the Pandemic Agreement and regional medicine production, and quietly resists US pressure it cannot afford to confront openly.

priorities.text: Promote universal public health systems over private insurance models, with health as a human right.
Regional and local medicine production, pooled purchasing through the PAHO Revolving Fund, and use of TRIPS flexibilities.
Complete the Pandemic Agreement and the PABS annex, from the moderate pro-equity middle ground of Latin America.
Strengthen PAHO and regional immunisation, especially against measles.
Protect the health of migrants moving through Mexico.

redLines.text: No language blaming migrants for spreading disease.
No conditions on health financing tied to security or trade.
No criticism of its centralised public health model.
No endorsement of US-style withdrawal or bilateral-only health deals.

interests.text: The government is centralising health care under the federal IMSS-Bienestar system, now covering 24 states, and announced 12,750 new primary care offices and a national network of public pharmacies from January 2027.

Officials claim 96% of medicines are in stock, but protests over hospital shortages continued in 2026. In April 2025 the state drug distributor Birmex’s tender was annulled over 13 billion pesos of overpricing and its director was removed.
Had the most measles cases in the Americas in 2025 (over 6,000). PAHO reviews Mexico’s measles elimination status in November 2026, just as Mexico prepares to co-host the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with Brazil, South Africa, Norway (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Multilateralist, procedural and moderate. Prefers consensus and regional coordination through PAHO and GRULAC. Avoids direct confrontation with the US. Principled and rights-based: ‘health is a right, not a privilege’, ‘the state must guarantee’. Measured tone, frequent references to Latin American solidarity.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.basis: team research reviewed 2026-10-17 (sources listed); key claims sample-checked 2026-11-27
profiles.summary: Nigeria demands that rich countries stop poaching its doctors and nurses without paying for them, insists on ending aid dependency on its own terms, and defends its religious and cultural values against what it sees as imported social agendas.

priorities.text: Make destination countries pay for the health workers they recruit: compensation, co-funded training, and a stronger WHO Code on international recruitment. Nigeria called for a new global migration framework in 2026.
End dependence on donors on Nigeria’s own terms: pooled procurement, local manufacturing (such as the lenacapavir HIV-prevention rollout) and the Lusaka Agenda.
Reform debt and international financing so that loan repayments stop crowding out health spending.
Stronger surveillance for outbreaks such as Lassa fever, cholera and mpox, and regional vaccine manufacturing through PABS benefit-sharing.

redLines.text: No language implying religious persecution or sectarian targeting in Nigeria’s health system.
No sexual and reproductive health rights or sexual orientation and gender identity language beyond previously agreed text; same-sex relations are criminalised in Nigeria.
No binding governance conditions attached to health aid.
No framing of health-worker emigration as Nigeria’s own fault; the burden should fall on recruiting countries.

interests.text: US cuts in 2025 removed about 92% of USAID funding to Nigeria; PEPFAR had provided about US$680 million a year.

Lawmakers approved US$200 million in 2025 to offset the cuts, and President Tinubu approved US$346 million in co-financing for HIV, TB and malaria in 2026. The government said it would absorb 28,000 health workers previously paid by USAID.
Health received about 5% of the 2025 federal budget, far below the 15% Abuja target. The minister admitted only ₦36 million of a ₦218 billion health capital budget was actually released in 2025.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with South Africa, Kenya, DR Congo, Saudi Arabia, Russia (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Assertive regional heavyweight that wants to lead the Africa Group. Pragmatic and transactional with donors, and aligns with conservative states on social issues. Confident and direct. Talks about Africa’s ‘self-reliance’, the ‘brain drain’ and fairness. Willing to name rich countries that recruit its health workers.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.basis: team research reviewed 2026-10-17 (sources listed); key claims sample-checked 2026-11-27
profiles.summary: Norway is WHO’s most reliable flexible funder and a champion of reproductive rights and accountability, but in the pathogen-sharing talks it sides with the pharmaceutical industry against binding benefit-sharing, and it is quietly abandoning its 1% aid target.

priorities.text: Sustainable, flexible WHO financing, including higher mandatory contributions from all members.
A more transparent and accountable WHO.
Strong emergency response capacity.
Protect and expand sexual and reproductive health and rights.
Health system strengthening and innovation through CEPI and the Lusaka Agenda.

redLines.text: No retreat on sexual and reproductive health and rights or gender language.
No mandatory registration of users of pathogen sequence databases.
No standardised binding contracts in PABS; the system must stay ‘sufficiently attractive’ to pharmaceutical companies.

interests.text: The 2027 draft budget sets aid at 0.93% of national income, effectively dropping the 1% target, and cuts Africa funding; over 30% of aid goes to Ukraine and refugee costs in Norway.

Provided over 46% of WHO’s Contingency Fund for Emergencies in 2025, gave NOK 1 billion to the WHO Investment Round, NOK 50 million for the Ebola response, and NOK 10 billion to Gavi and the Global Fund for 2026–30.
Kept funding for sexual and reproductive health steady, including about NOK 590 million to UNFPA.

partners.text: Often aligned on this agenda with United Kingdom, Germany, France, Kenya, Mexico, Brazil (team research) — decide each proposal on its clauses, not on who moved it.

profiles.style: Earnest ‘honest broker’. Uses its funding weight to push WHO reform and accountability, works closely with Nordic and EU partners, and holds firm on reproductive rights and PABS. Plain-spoken, data-driven and principled. Willing to criticise WHO governance while bankrolling it. Talks about ‘flexible funding’, ‘accountability’ and ‘rights for all’.
caveats: Profile is team research; figures marked unverified must be hedged.

profiles.basis: team research reviewed 2026-10-17 (sources listed); key claims sample-checked 2026-11-27
profiles.summary: The Russian Federation opposes the ‘politicisation’ of WHO, rejects any supranational authority over sovereign health decisions, attacks Western hypocrisy over abandoned aid and sanctions, and offers itself to Africa as an alternative partner in outbreak response.

priorities.text: Stop WHO from being used to condemn Russia over Ukraine, which it calls ‘politicisation’ of a technical health body.
Get language recognising that unilateral sanctions harm access to medicines and medical equipment, and seek exemptions.
Expand bilateral health influence in Africa (laboratories, test kits, training) as an alternative to Western aid.
Keep strong sovereignty language in the Pandemic Agreement, IHR and PABS annex, and resist any outside oversight.
Remove ‘gender’, sexual orientation and comprehensive sexuality education language from health texts, in favour of ‘traditional family values’.

redLines.text: Any text attributing attacks on health care to Russia or calling for accountability mechanisms.
Any binding compliance, inspection or verification powers for WHO.
‘Gender-responsive’, sexual orientation and gender identity, or comprehensive sexuality education language.
Institutional penalties against Russia within WHO, such as relocating the European office or suspending its rights.

chunks.title: Bangladesh: position on health financing
chunks.text: Bangladesh insists that the health of over a million Rohingya refugees is a global responsibility, not Bangladesh’s burden, and fights to keep the patent flexibilities that protect its generic medicine industry. Objectives: Predictable, multi-year international funding for refugee health as a shared global responsibility.; Keep or extend TRIPS patent flexibilities and support compulsory licensing to protect its generics industry.; PABS benefit-sharing and technology transfer for regional manufacturing.; Recognition of climate change as a health threat, and support for the Pandemic Fund.; Continued access to grants and soft loans despite rising income.. Red lines: No language implying the Rohingya should be integrated or permanently settled in Bangladesh.; No shifting of refugee health costs onto the Bangladeshi budget.; No ‘TRIPS-plus’ intellectual property obligations.; No criticism of Bangladesh’s post-2024 political transition..

chunks.title: Bangladesh: national context
chunks.text: Hosts over a million Rohingya refugees from Myanmar in Cox’s Bazar. The 2026 UN response plan asks for US$710.5 million, 26% less than 2025. The US cut about US$200 million in early 2025, and at least 11 health centres closed in 18 months, leaving about 300,000 refugees without nearby care.

chunks.title: Bangladesh: national context
chunks.text: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman presented a five-point plan at the UN General Assembly in September 2026 demanding a roadmap for Rohingya repatriation and ‘predictable funding’.

chunks.title: Bangladesh: national context
chunks.text: Is due to graduate from Least Developed Country status on 4 Nov 2026; the BNP government asked the UN to defer it. Graduation would end Bangladesh’s exemption from WTO drug-patent rules, threatening its large generic pharmaceutical export industry and raising medicine prices.

chunks.title: Bangladesh: national context
chunks.text: The government claims to have doubled the health budget, with plans for 20 new hospitals and 5,000 new doctors, and has sought wider health cooperation with China.

chunks.title: Bangladesh: national context
chunks.text: Faces climate-driven health threats such as floods and recurring dengue epidemics.

chunks.title: Bangladesh: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Pushes for Rohingya repatriation while conditions in Myanmar’s Rakhine State (civil war, Arakan Army control) make safe returns unrealistic. Critics say Dhaka uses donor fatigue as leverage.

chunks.title: Bangladesh: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Asks to delay LDC graduation while presenting itself as an economic success story.

chunks.title: Bangladesh: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Claims a ‘doubled’ health budget while public health spending remains among the lowest in Asia relative to the size of its economy.

chunks.title: Bangladesh: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Is moving closer to China while staying pragmatic with India and the US.

chunks.title: Brazil: position on health financing
chunks.text: Brazil champions universal public health systems, local production of vaccines and medicines, and a Pandemic Agreement that puts benefit-sharing on an equal footing with pathogen access, positioning itself as the Global South’s bridge-builder. Objectives: Conclude the PABS annex within 2026, with ‘equal footing between access and benefit sharing’ and no weakening of the 20% production commitment in Article 12.; Expand local and regional production of vaccines and medicines through technology transfer (the Fiocruz model and the PAHO Revolving Fund for pooled vaccine purchasing).; Promote universal public health systems like the SUS as the answer to collapsing aid, rather than donor-run disease programmes.; Link health to climate justice, hunger and poverty reduction.; Reform global health architecture to give the Global South more voice.. Red lines: No reopening of equity commitments already agreed in the Pandemic Agreement.; No PABS system where benefits are voluntary or come too late.; No intellectual property language restricting compulsory licensing. Brazil broke the patent on the HIV drug efavirenz in 2007 and is proud of it.; Under Lula, Brazil defends gender equality and sexual and reproductive health language against deletion.; No language condemning Russia by name..

chunks.title: Brazil: national context
chunks.text: Brazil’s Unified Health System (SUS) provides free universal care to over 200 million people and is Lula’s showcase model.

chunks.title: Brazil: national context
chunks.text: Law 15.471 of 20 July 2026 created a national strategy to produce more vaccines and medicines domestically (Health Economic-Industrial Complex).

chunks.title: Brazil: national context
chunks.text: Hosted COP30 in Belém (November 2025); its Health Ministry presented the draft Belém Health Action Plan, linking climate and health, in Brasília in July 2025.

chunks.title: Brazil: national context
chunks.text: Chaired BRICS in 2025, and the BRICS Vaccine R&D Centre met in Brazil.

chunks.title: Brazil: national context
chunks.text: Pushed to finish the PABS annex in 2026 (with Botswana); the EU expects talks to run into 2027.

chunks.title: Brazil: national context
chunks.text: Abstained on WHA79/11, the resolution on the health impact of Russia’s war in Ukraine.

chunks.title: Brazil: national context
chunks.text: Faces a heavy domestic dengue burden, which strains the SUS.

chunks.title: Brazil: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its ‘equity’ stance overlaps with industrial policy: technology transfer would benefit Brazilian manufacturers like Fiocruz.

chunks.title: Brazil: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Claims to champion humanitarian law but stays neutral on Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian hospitals, which draws Western criticism.

chunks.title: Brazil: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Lula won the 25 Oct 2026 presidential runoff (about 51.8%) and begins a fourth term in January 2027; Flávio Bolsonaro has not conceded and seeks annulment, so continuity is likely but contested.

chunks.title: Brazil: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Showcases the SUS abroad while it struggles at home with waiting lists, underfunding and dengue epidemics.

chunks.title: Brazil: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Reversed Bolsonaro’s decision to join the anti-abortion Geneva Consensus Declaration in 2023, so its reproductive health stance depends entirely on who governs.

chunks.title: China: position on health financing
chunks.text: China advocates for equitable global health cooperation that strengthens developing countries’ healthcare capacity, promotes access to medical technology, and respects national sovereignty and non-interference in domestic affairs. Objectives: Champion WHO’s ‘central coordinating role’ and multilateralism, presenting China as the responsible power in contrast to US withdrawal.; Reform global health governance so developing countries get more voice and representation.; Press developed countries to ‘fulfil their financial obligations’ and restore aid, while framing China’s own contributions as South-South solidarity rather than donor charity.; Strengthen health systems in developing countries through workforce training, medical technology sharing, and access to essential medicines and vaccines.; In the PABS talks, back legally certain benefit-sharing rules alongside the developing-country camp.; Expand bilateral health cooperation (Africa CDC, BRICS vaccine centre, Chinese medical teams) as an alternative to Western aid.. Red lines: No participation by Taiwan ‘in any form’: no observer status, no references to Taiwan’s health system or data-sharing.; No new COVID-origins investigations, lab audits or WHO verification on Chinese territory without its consent.; No resolutions that name or condemn Russia.; No international health initiatives it sees as politically motivated or as interfering in internal affairs, including human rights language aimed at Xinjiang or Tibet.; No intellectual property arrangements that restrict developing countries’ access to medical technology, and no dues formula that makes China the top payer without matching influence..

chunks.title: China: national context
chunks.text: Pledged US$500 million to WHO over five years in May 2025, becoming its largest state donor after the US exit. The pledge mixes higher assessed dues, voluntary money and South-South projects; how much has been paid out is unclear.

chunks.title: China: national context
chunks.text: In Feb 2025 China was one of only two states that opposed the 20% increase in WHO assessed contributions, citing a sluggish global economy. Under the new UN scale its share of dues rises from about 15% to 20%.

chunks.title: China: national context
chunks.text: WHA79 (May 2026) again refused to invite Taiwan as an observer, the 10th year in a row, with China and Pakistan opposing.

chunks.title: China: national context
chunks.text: WHO’s expert group on the origins of COVID-19 (SAGO) said in June 2025 it could not reach a conclusion because China had not shared early genetic sequences and lab biosafety data.

chunks.title: China: national context
chunks.text: Sent an Ebola expert team to Kinshasa in June 2026 and says it has 45 medical teams working in 44 African countries.

chunks.title: China: national context
chunks.text: Voted against WHA79/11, the resolution on the health impact of Russia’s war in Ukraine.

chunks.title: China: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Fills the funding vacuum with influence-building money, yet resisted the very dues increase that funds WHO’s core budget. Critics see the US$500m pledge as buying influence rather than solidarity.

chunks.title: China: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its record on transparency (SARS in 2003, the first weeks of COVID-19, refusing SAGO’s data requests) sits awkwardly with its rhetoric about outbreak preparedness and early warning.

chunks.title: China: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Calls claims that excluding Taiwan leaves a surveillance gap a ‘political lie’, while Taiwan says it is cut off from real-time WHO information.

chunks.title: China: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): As a major producer of pharmaceutical ingredients and vaccines, China is also a user of pathogen samples in PABS, so its ‘equity’ position is partly commercial.

chunks.title: China: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Health aid often comes packaged with Belt and Road infrastructure, loans and diplomatic expectations (such as cutting ties with Taiwan).

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: position on health financing
chunks.text: The DRC advocates for equitable access to healthcare through sustained international funding, strengthened domestic healthcare infrastructure, and coordinated disease prevention efforts that respect national sovereignty. Objectives: Increased international financial and technical assistance to strengthen healthcare infrastructure, train medical personnel, improve disease surveillance and provide emergency medical supplies.; Fast, flexible emergency money for the Ebola response, through WHO’s contingency fund, the Pandemic Fund and donors, channelled through the government: ‘one plan, one team, one budget’.; Research, development and fair access for Bundibugyo vaccines and treatments, with trials run in the DRC and benefits returned to the DRC.; A strong PABS benefit-sharing system, since samples from the DRC have fed vaccine development before without guaranteed returns.; WHO coordination and international cooperation to contain outbreaks before they cross borders, including protection for health workers and humanitarian access in conflict zones.. Red lines: Preserve national sovereignty and control over domestic healthcare decisions; no parallel aid structures run by NGOs that bypass the Health Ministry.; No discriminatory travel restrictions against Congolese people (such as Saudi Arabia’s Ebola visa ban).; No language implying the government is incapable or corrupt.; No text that treats Rwanda or M23 as neutral actors, or that ignores how the conflict drives the epidemic.; No emergency responses that undermine long-term health system development, and no sharing of samples without benefits returned..

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: national context
chunks.text: Is fighting the largest Ebola outbreak in its history: the Bundibugyo strain, declared on 15 May 2026 in Ituri and declared a global health emergency (PHEIC) by WHO on 17 May. By mid-October 2026 there were roughly 9,000 confirmed cases and 4,400 deaths across seven provinces. There is no licensed vaccine or treatment for this strain.

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: national context
chunks.text: Has handled 16 earlier Ebola outbreaks and presents itself as the world’s most experienced Ebola responder.

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: national context
chunks.text: Before the cuts, USAID gave the DRC over US$1 billion a year (2023), mostly for health and humanitarian work. The US funded over 70% of humanitarian action in the country in 2024.

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: national context
chunks.text: Signed a bilateral health agreement with the US on 26 Feb 2026 under the ‘America First’ strategy: up to US$900 million from the US and US$300 million from the DRC over five years, focused on disease surveillance and laboratories. It sits alongside a US-brokered peace process with Rwanda and a US minerals partnership.

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: national context
chunks.text: Fighting in the east involving the M23 rebel group, which the DRC and UN experts say is backed by Rwanda, continued into 2026 despite peace accords. The conflict zones overlap with the Ebola epicentre.

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: national context
chunks.text: Spent about 13% of its 2025 budget on health, below the 15% Abuja target.

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Government spokesman Patrick Muyaya hit back at NGO critics in June 2026, suggesting some use the epidemic to raise money, and complained that US funding goes to NGOs rather than the state.

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Ebola response workers in Bunia protested over unpaid bonuses in July 2026. Earlier Ebola responses (2018–20) had well-documented misuse of funds, which makes donors wary of handing the government control of the money.

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Demands sovereignty while depending on donors for most outbreak financing.

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its US health deal sits alongside a minerals-for-security arrangement, which critics call transactional.

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Ebola spreads partly because insecurity, community distrust of responders and attacks on health workers in the east have never been resolved.

chunks.title: France: position on health financing
chunks.text: France speaks grandly of multilateralism, One Health and reforming the global health architecture, and defends reproductive rights as part of its ‘feminist diplomacy’, while making the deepest aid cuts in the G7. Objectives: Reform of the ‘global health architecture’ led from Europe.; A ‘One Health’ approach linking human, animal and environmental health.; Finalise the Pandemic Agreement and PABS annex.; Champion multilateralism against US unilateralism.; Support Africa CDC and local African production, especially in francophone Africa.; Defend sexual and reproductive health and rights and gender equality.. Red lines: No rollback of sexual and reproductive health or gender language.; No PABS terms that undermine the European pharmaceutical base or intellectual property.; No new financial commitments that parliament will not pass..

chunks.title: France: national context
chunks.text: The 2026 budget, forced through without a parliamentary vote, cut aid by about €800 million (−18%). Aid in 2025 was €12.9 billion, 0.42% of national income, the lowest since 2017. The 2027 draft budget cuts it again; aid credits have roughly halved in three years.

chunks.title: France: national context
chunks.text: Cut its Global Fund pledge for 2026–28 by 58% and Unitaid by 22%.

chunks.title: France: national context
chunks.text: President Macron hosted the One Health Summit in Lyon in April 2026, where NGOs protested the ‘amputation’ of France’s Global Fund contribution. France also hosts the WHO Academy in Lyon.

chunks.title: France: national context
chunks.text: Has deep ties with francophone Africa, including the DRC.

chunks.title: France: national context
chunks.text: Supported Taiwan’s participation at WHA79.

chunks.title: France: national context
chunks.text: As an EU member, is part of the bloc that resists binding benefit-sharing contracts in PABS, despite France’s equity rhetoric. Home to Sanofi and the Institut Pasteur.

chunks.title: France: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Macron’s summit rhetoric contrasts with France having the steepest aid cuts in the G7.

chunks.title: France: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Domestic budget crisis and pressure from the far-right Rassemblement National, which favours further aid cuts.

chunks.title: France: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its equity rhetoric sits uneasily with the EU’s resistance to binding PABS contracts.

chunks.title: France: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its influence in francophone Africa is shrinking, especially in the Sahel, where Russia has replaced it as a security partner.

chunks.title: Germany: position on health financing
chunks.text: Germany wants a lean, efficient WHO focused on its core mandate and a pathogen-sharing system that keeps pharmaceutical research attractive, while it cuts development aid to pay for defence and calls itself WHO’s most reliable funder. Objectives: A ‘strong WHO that focuses on its core competencies’: norms and standards, health security and coordination.; WHO reform and efficiency in return for continued funding.; Prioritise antimicrobial resistance and health security.; A PABS system that works for industry, with pathogens kept out of the Nagoya biodiversity protocol’s rules.; Act as a bridge-builder within the EU.. Red lines: No mandatory, standardised benefit-sharing contracts that ‘stifle R&D’.; No weakening of intellectual property or TRIPS protections.; No open-ended new spending commitments.; No retreat on gender equality and sexual and reproductive health language..

chunks.title: Germany: national context
chunks.text: After the US exit, Germany says it is WHO’s largest financial contributor. At WHA79 it pledged an extra €25 million, mainly for cross-border outbreaks.

chunks.title: Germany: national context
chunks.text: The development ministry’s core budget has fallen from €12.4 billion (2021) to €9.9 billion (2026), and the 2027 plan cuts it by a further 5.8%. The government dropped the 0.7% aid target and ended bilateral health cooperation with partner countries.

chunks.title: Germany: national context
chunks.text: Funding for the WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence in Berlin was halved from about €30m a year to €15m, with only one year committed (Health Policy Watch, 8 Jan 2026).

chunks.title: Germany: national context
chunks.text: Pledged €1 billion to the Global Fund for 2026–28, about 23% less than last time.

chunks.title: Germany: national context
chunks.text: The 2027 federal budget grows almost 6%, mostly for defence.

chunks.title: Germany: national context
chunks.text: Supported Taiwan’s observer participation at WHA79.

chunks.title: Germany: national context
chunks.text: Speaks through the EU in the PABS negotiations, where the EU resists binding benefit-sharing contracts.

chunks.title: Germany: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): A TU Dresden scholar calls Germany’s medicines policy ‘organised hypocrisy’: it supports equity in Geneva but blocks it in trade negotiations.

chunks.title: Germany: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Analysts describe heavy pharmaceutical industry lobbying (BioNTech, Bayer, Boehringer Ingelheim) shaping its PABS position.

chunks.title: Germany: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Has no working global health strategy or coordinator, and the Bundestag let its global health subcommittee lapse.

chunks.title: Germany: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Defence spending is crowding out aid.

chunks.title: Germany: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Paid about €400 million in subsidies to keep Sanofi’s insulin production in Frankfurt: domestic supply security comes first.

chunks.title: Germany: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Actively recruits nurses from abroad, including from countries with shortages.

chunks.title: India: position on health financing
chunks.text: India demands a fair, legally binding pandemic system that guarantees the Global South access to vaccines, medicines and technology, protects generic manufacturing, and positions India as the world’s affordable pharmacy without accepting outside intrusion into its sovereignty. Objectives: PABS: standardised, legally binding contracts at the point of pathogen access, with digital traceability of samples and sequence data.; Equitable access to vaccines, tests and treatments through technology transfer and regional manufacturing, with India as a central hub.; Protect generic medicine production and TRIPS flexibilities, including compulsory licensing.; Bring traditional medicine (Ayush) into WHO frameworks for primary health care and universal health coverage.; Promote India’s digital public health infrastructure (such as the CoWIN vaccination platform and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission) as a global public good.. Red lines: No language that restricts TRIPS flexibilities, compulsory licensing or generic manufacturing.; No intrusive verification, compliance reviews or WHO powers that override national decisions.; No PABS deal that gives pharmaceutical companies free access to pathogens without enforceable benefits for developing countries.; No resolutions naming Russia (abstained on WHA79/11).; No criticism of Indian drug quality that could be used to justify trade barriers against Indian generics..

chunks.title: India: national context
chunks.text: The central health ministry’s 2026–27 budget is about ₹1.02 lakh crore: 1.96% of central government spending and under 0.3% of GDP. The 2017 target of 2.5% of GDP in public health spending (all levels of government) by 2025 was missed.

chunks.title: India: national context
chunks.text: Voted for the Pandemic Agreement in May 2025. Modi addressed WHA78, promoting the Ayushman Bharat insurance scheme and low-cost public pharmacies as models for the Global South.

chunks.title: India: national context
chunks.text: Hosts the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre in Jamnagar and co-hosted the 2nd WHO Global Summit on Traditional Medicine in December 2025.

chunks.title: India: national context
chunks.text: In October 2025 WHO issued an alert after contaminated Indian cough syrups killed more than 20 children in Madhya Pradesh, following earlier deaths linked to Indian syrups in Gambia and Uzbekistan in 2022–23.

chunks.title: India: national context
chunks.text: Chairs BRICS in 2026 and hosted the BRICS health ministers (July) and summit (September).

chunks.title: India: national context
chunks.text: At the UN high-level meeting in September 2026, India said the Pandemic Agreement’s credibility depends on a fair PABS system.

chunks.title: India: national context
chunks.text: The Serum Institute of India is manufacturing the Oxford candidate vaccine for the Bundibugyo Ebola strain now in trials.

chunks.title: India: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Calls itself the ‘pharmacy of the world’, while repeated contaminated-medicine scandals have damaged trust in its regulators.

chunks.title: India: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Demands that rich countries fund global health equity, while its own public health spending is among the lowest of any large economy and out-of-pocket costs remain high.

chunks.title: India: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its push for ‘equity’ also serves industrial policy: Indian vaccine makers like the Serum Institute want pathogen access and technology transfer too.

chunks.title: India: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Promotes traditional medicine at WHO despite criticism that much of it lacks strong scientific evidence.

chunks.title: India: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its ‘Vaccine Maitri’ vaccine diplomacy was suddenly halted by export bans during India’s 2021 COVID wave, and African countries remember the shortfall.

chunks.title: India: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Balances between camps: Global South champion with China and Russia in BRICS, but also partners with the US and Japan in the Quad and is wary of Chinese influence in WHO.

chunks.title: Indonesia: position on health financing
chunks.text: Indonesia leads the developing world’s demand for a legally binding pathogen-sharing system with guaranteed benefits, while courting donors and the US as its health minister campaigns to become WHO’s next Director-General. Objectives: A legally binding, enforceable PABS annex that starts operating together with the Pandemic Agreement, with nothing left to be decided later.; Real benefit-sharing: about 20% of pandemic products reserved for WHO, annual payments from companies that use the system, and no anonymous users of pathogen data.; Local and regional vaccine and biotech manufacturing (such as the state company Bio Farma) and technology transfer.; A leaner, more ‘useful’ WHO focused on core work and funded partly by development banks, with countries moving from grants to loans to domestic financing.; Keep the door open to the US re-engaging with global health.. Red lines: No PABS annex that merely repeats Article 12 of the Agreement or contains ‘major loopholes’.; No pathogen sharing without guaranteed benefits.; No delay in making the PABS system operational..

chunks.title: Indonesia: national context
chunks.text: Founded and leads the Group for Equity, a coalition of over 30 developing countries in the PABS negotiations, and coordinates with the Africa Group.

chunks.title: Indonesia: national context
chunks.text: In 2007 Indonesia refused to share H5N1 bird flu samples until it was guaranteed access to resulting vaccines, the episode that started the global debate on benefit-sharing.

chunks.title: Indonesia: national context
chunks.text: The Pandemic Fund was launched under Indonesia’s G20 presidency in 2022.

chunks.title: Indonesia: national context
chunks.text: At home: a free health check programme (over 70 million people screened by January 2026, according to the government) and an extra Rp20 trillion (about US$1.2 billion) for the national health insurer BPJS in 2026.

chunks.title: Indonesia: national context
chunks.text: Prabowo’s huge free school meals programme dominates the budget and has been hit by thousands of food poisoning cases.

chunks.title: Indonesia: national context
chunks.text: Health Minister Budi says he has raised US$8.5 billion from development banks and argues WHO should use ‘other people’s money’.

chunks.title: Indonesia: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Budi’s campaign for Director-General shapes everything: Indonesia is hard-line on PABS to keep Global South votes, but conciliatory toward donors and the US to win Northern votes. Budi says he knows US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. personally.

chunks.title: Indonesia: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): His case for a leaner WHO and loan-based financing does not go down well with the poorest countries, which need grants.

chunks.title: Indonesia: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): At home, spending prioritises the free meals programme despite its food safety failures; Prabowo claimed a ‘99.99%’ success rate.

chunks.title: Indonesia: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its 2023 Health Law was opposed by medical associations.

chunks.title: Indonesia: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Uses its ‘non-aligned’ identity strategically to stay friends with everyone.

chunks.title: Japan: position on health financing
chunks.text: Japan frames everything through universal health coverage and ‘human security’, pushing countries toward self-reliant health financing, while it halves its global health pledges, funds record defence spending and stands firm against China over Taiwan. Objectives: Universal health coverage and ‘human security’ as the organising frame for global health.; Move countries toward domestic resource mobilisation and self-reliant health financing.; Health security and emergency preparedness, including through the UHC Knowledge Hub.; A PABS system that preserves incentives for research and development.; Resilient medical supply chains as part of economic security.. Red lines: No mandatory technology transfer or intellectual property waivers.; No binding financing targets.; No language that legitimises China’s position on Taiwan..

chunks.title: Japan: national context
chunks.text: FY2026 defence budget is a record ¥9.04 trillion, about 2% of GDP.

chunks.title: Japan: national context
chunks.text: Pledged up to ¥81 billion (about US$515 million) to the Global Fund for 2026–28 — about half its previous pledge in dollar terms (about 20% less in yen).

chunks.title: Japan: national context
chunks.text: Co-founded the UHC Knowledge Hub with the World Bank and WHO in Tokyo (December 2025), now supporting eight countries. Co-hosted a side event on UHC financing with Nigeria at WHA79.

chunks.title: Japan: national context
chunks.text: Relations with China have been sharply tense since Takaichi said in November 2025 that a Taiwan crisis could threaten Japan’s survival; Beijing demanded a retraction and applied economic pressure.

chunks.title: Japan: national context
chunks.text: Backed Taiwan’s participation in WHO in a joint statement in May 2026.

chunks.title: Japan: national context
chunks.text: Home to major pharmaceutical companies such as Takeda and Daiichi Sankyo.

chunks.title: Japan: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Pledged up to ¥81 billion (about US$515 million) to the Global Fund for 2026–28 — about half its previous pledge in dollar terms (about 20% less in yen).

chunks.title: Japan: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Recruits caregivers and nurses from Southeast Asia to staff its ageing society while remaining cautious about immigration.

chunks.title: Japan: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its ‘self-reliance’ message can sound like an excuse for donors to pay less.

chunks.title: Japan: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Close to the US bilaterally, but stays in WHO and avoids criticising Washington’s withdrawal openly.

chunks.title: Kenya: position on health financing
chunks.text: Kenya presents itself as Africa’s model of ‘ownership’ and co-financing, the reliable partner that can work with Washington and Geneva at once, while defending the bilateral deals and health-worker exports that critics say undercut African solidarity. Objectives: Showcase Kenya’s ‘co-financing and transition’ model and attract investment, including regional headquarters and vaccine manufacturing.; Domestic financing for universal health coverage through the SHA, plus debt relief and fairer international financing.; Stronger Africa CDC, regional manufacturing and pooled procurement.; ‘Managed’ health-worker migration that pays back through remittances or training funds, not restrictions.; Data sovereignty language that does not threaten its US agreement.. Red lines: No text implying that bilateral data and sample-sharing deals undermine the multilateral PABS system.; No restrictions on health-worker mobility; Kenya benefits from remittances.; No criticism of the SHA’s governance.; No binding obligations without flexibility on co-financing..

chunks.title: Kenya: national context
chunks.text: USAID gave Kenya about US$470 million a year in 2020–25, roughly 80% of it for health.

chunks.title: Kenya: national context
chunks.text: Was the first African country to sign a US ‘America First’ health deal (4 Dec 2025): about US$1.6 billion from the US over five years, with US$850 million of Kenyan co-financing rising each year.

chunks.title: Kenya: national context
chunks.text: The deal includes sharing of medical records, genomic and pathogen data, and biological samples with the US. Kenya’s High Court froze it in December 2025; the Court of Appeal allowed it to proceed on 9 Oct 2026, but the constitutional case continues.

chunks.title: Kenya: national context
chunks.text: Its new national health insurer, the Social Health Authority (SHA), faces debt disputes with private hospitals (over Ksh43 billion claimed in 2025), and over 1,000 facilities were shut over fraud. The opposition calls it near collapse.

chunks.title: Kenya: national context
chunks.text: President Ruto openly promotes exporting nurses, with labour deals with the UK, Germany and Gulf states.

chunks.title: Kenya: national context
chunks.text: Confirmed an imported Bundibugyo Ebola case on 6 Oct 2026; no local spread reported.

chunks.title: Kenya: national context
chunks.text: Co-chaired the Lusaka Agenda process on reforming global health initiatives.

chunks.title: Kenya: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Sharing genomic data and specimens bilaterally with the US, without binding benefit-sharing, contradicts the Africa Group’s own PABS position.

chunks.title: Kenya: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): The US deal was published only after signing, and parliament never approved the US$850 million co-financing commitment.

chunks.title: Kenya: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Exports nurses while its own public hospitals are short of staff; only a fraction of new graduates get local jobs.

chunks.title: Kenya: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Chaos at the SHA and unpaid hospital bills undercut its universal health coverage rhetoric.

chunks.title: Kenya: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): A designated major non-NATO ally of the US, while trying to stay credible inside the Africa Group, some of whose members (such as Zambia and Zimbabwe) resisted US data-sharing terms.

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: position on health financing
chunks.text: The Republic of Korea offers its COVID-19 response expertise and biomanufacturing know-how as a bridge between donors and developing countries, while cutting humanitarian aid in half and funding visible WHO projects that also promote its own bio industry. Objectives: Strengthen health security and emergency response, drawing on Korea’s COVID-19 experience (testing, tracing, digital tools).; Build biomanufacturing capacity in developing countries through training and partnerships.; Support WHO reform and efficiency during budget cuts.; Promote digital health.; Act as a bridge between donors and developing countries.. Red lines: No PABS terms that burden export-oriented Korean vaccine and biologics manufacturers.; No hard financing targets after its aid cuts.; Avoid antagonising either China or the US..

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: national context
chunks.text: The Foreign Ministry's 2025 budget proposal cut its ODA by about 22% (KRW 2.81tn to 2.19tn) and humanitarian aid by about 51% (Korea Herald, 29 Aug 2025).

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: national context
chunks.text: President Lee ordered a review of whether aid projects serve ‘national prestige and diplomatic goals’, amid a probe into alleged aid-related influence-peddling involving the former first lady.

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: national context
chunks.text: Funded the JW Lee Strategic Situation Room at WHO headquarters (opened May 2026), named after Lee Jong-wook, the Korean WHO Director-General who died in office in 2006.

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: national context
chunks.text: Hosts the WHO Global Training Hub for Biomanufacturing, which has trained about 4,000 people from 79 countries.

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: national context
chunks.text: Pledged US$100 million to the Global Fund for 2026–28.

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: national context
chunks.text: Took a seat on the WHO Executive Board in 2026.

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: national context
chunks.text: Home to major vaccine and biologics makers such as Samsung Biologics and SK bioscience.

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Funds high-visibility WHO projects bearing Korean names while halving humanitarian aid.

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its ‘capacity-building’ in biomanufacturing also opens markets and partnerships for the Korean bio industry.

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Stays silent on Taiwan; Korea did not join the countries backing Taiwan’s participation at WHA79.

chunks.title: Republic of Korea: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): At home, a long and bitter conflict between the government and doctors over medical school admissions disrupted hospitals.

chunks.title: Mexico: position on health financing
chunks.text: Mexico defends health as a right delivered by a strong public state, backs the Pandemic Agreement and regional medicine production, and quietly resists US pressure it cannot afford to confront openly. Objectives: Promote universal public health systems over private insurance models, with health as a human right.; Regional and local medicine production, pooled purchasing through the PAHO Revolving Fund, and use of TRIPS flexibilities.; Complete the Pandemic Agreement and the PABS annex, from the moderate pro-equity middle ground of Latin America.; Strengthen PAHO and regional immunisation, especially against measles.; Protect the health of migrants moving through Mexico.. Red lines: No language blaming migrants for spreading disease.; No conditions on health financing tied to security or trade.; No criticism of its centralised public health model.; No endorsement of US-style withdrawal or bilateral-only health deals..

chunks.title: Mexico: national context
chunks.text: The government is centralising health care under the federal IMSS-Bienestar system, now covering 24 states, and announced 12,750 new primary care offices and a national network of public pharmacies from January 2027.

chunks.title: Mexico: national context
chunks.text: Officials claim 96% of medicines are in stock, but protests over hospital shortages continued in 2026. In April 2025 the state drug distributor Birmex’s tender was annulled over 13 billion pesos of overpricing and its director was removed.

chunks.title: Mexico: national context
chunks.text: Had the most measles cases in the Americas in 2025 (over 6,000). PAHO reviews Mexico’s measles elimination status in November 2026, just as Mexico prepares to co-host the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

chunks.title: Mexico: national context
chunks.text: Relations with the US are dominated by tariffs, migration and fentanyl. President Sheinbaum has blamed the US opioid crisis partly on US drug regulators. Mexico was barely affected by USAID cuts.

chunks.title: Mexico: national context
chunks.text: ‘Plan México’ favours drug companies that manufacture in Mexico for public procurement in 2026–28.

chunks.title: Mexico: national context
chunks.text: The health minister did not attend WHA79; a lower-level delegation went instead.

chunks.title: Mexico: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Claims near-full medicine supply while shortages persist. Critics trace them to the centralised procurement begun under former President López Obrador, which Sheinbaum continues.

chunks.title: Mexico: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its ‘self-sufficiency’ agenda relies on the same state company (Birmex) that was caught in an overpricing scandal.

chunks.title: Mexico: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Vaccination gaps behind the measles resurgence threaten its elimination status during the World Cup.

chunks.title: Mexico: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Depends heavily on trade with the US, so it criticises the US withdrawal only quietly.

chunks.title: Mexico: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Sent a lower-profile delegation to WHA79, signalling reduced engagement despite multilateralist rhetoric.

chunks.title: Nigeria: position on health financing
chunks.text: Nigeria demands that rich countries stop poaching its doctors and nurses without paying for them, insists on ending aid dependency on its own terms, and defends its religious and cultural values against what it sees as imported social agendas. Objectives: Make destination countries pay for the health workers they recruit: compensation, co-funded training, and a stronger WHO Code on international recruitment. Nigeria called for a new global migration framework in 2026.; End dependence on donors on Nigeria’s own terms: pooled procurement, local manufacturing (such as the lenacapavir HIV-prevention rollout) and the Lusaka Agenda.; Reform debt and international financing so that loan repayments stop crowding out health spending.; Stronger surveillance for outbreaks such as Lassa fever, cholera and mpox, and regional vaccine manufacturing through PABS benefit-sharing.. Red lines: No language implying religious persecution or sectarian targeting in Nigeria’s health system.; No sexual and reproductive health rights or sexual orientation and gender identity language beyond previously agreed text; same-sex relations are criminalised in Nigeria.; No binding governance conditions attached to health aid.; No framing of health-worker emigration as Nigeria’s own fault; the burden should fall on recruiting countries..

chunks.title: Nigeria: national context
chunks.text: US cuts in 2025 removed about 92% of USAID funding to Nigeria; PEPFAR had provided about US$680 million a year.

chunks.title: Nigeria: national context
chunks.text: Lawmakers approved US$200 million in 2025 to offset the cuts, and President Tinubu approved US$346 million in co-financing for HIV, TB and malaria in 2026. The government said it would absorb 28,000 health workers previously paid by USAID.

chunks.title: Nigeria: national context
chunks.text: Health received about 5% of the 2025 federal budget, far below the 15% Abuja target. The minister admitted only ₦36 million of a ₦218 billion health capital budget was actually released in 2025.

chunks.title: Nigeria: national context
chunks.text: Signed a US$5.1 billion bilateral health deal with the US in December 2025 (about US$2.1 billion from the US, US$3 billion from Nigeria), including about US$200 million earmarked for over 900 Christian faith-based facilities. The US can pause the deal if Nigeria diverges from US interests.

chunks.title: Nigeria: national context
chunks.text: The US re-designated Nigeria a ‘Country of Particular Concern’ for religious freedom in November 2025, President Trump spoke of ‘Christian genocide’, and US strikes hit the northwest in December 2025, which Nigeria described as a joint operation.

chunks.title: Nigeria: national context
chunks.text: Is a major source of health workers for the UK: over 13,000 went in 2021–22, and Nigeria was the UK’s second-largest source of new nurses in 2025–26.

chunks.title: Nigeria: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Makes big budget promises but releases very little of the money (the ₦36 million figure).

chunks.title: Nigeria: team analysis
