chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Cut its 2025 family planning budget by 97% just as donor funding dried up.

chunks.title: Nigeria: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Officially rejects the US ‘Christian genocide’ narrative while accepting a US deal with funding earmarked for Christian facilities.

chunks.title: Nigeria: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Blames UK recruitment while doctors’ unions reject the government’s own proposals to restrict emigration, such as a five-year service bond.

chunks.title: Nigeria: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Claims over 90% of health spending is domestic, while other reports say its HIV response is about 80% donor-funded.

chunks.title: Norway: position on health financing
chunks.text: Norway is WHO’s most reliable flexible funder and a champion of reproductive rights and accountability, but in the pathogen-sharing talks it sides with the pharmaceutical industry against binding benefit-sharing, and it is quietly abandoning its 1% aid target. Objectives: Sustainable, flexible WHO financing, including higher mandatory contributions from all members.; A more transparent and accountable WHO.; Strong emergency response capacity.; Protect and expand sexual and reproductive health and rights.; Health system strengthening and innovation through CEPI and the Lusaka Agenda.. Red lines: No retreat on sexual and reproductive health and rights or gender language.; No mandatory registration of users of pathogen sequence databases.; No standardised binding contracts in PABS; the system must stay ‘sufficiently attractive’ to pharmaceutical companies..

chunks.title: Norway: national context
chunks.text: The 2027 draft budget sets aid at 0.93% of national income, effectively dropping the 1% target, and cuts Africa funding; over 30% of aid goes to Ukraine and refugee costs in Norway.

chunks.title: Norway: national context
chunks.text: Provided over 46% of WHO’s Contingency Fund for Emergencies in 2025, gave NOK 1 billion to the WHO Investment Round, NOK 50 million for the Ebola response, and NOK 10 billion to Gavi and the Global Fund for 2026–30.

chunks.title: Norway: national context
chunks.text: Kept funding for sexual and reproductive health steady, including about NOK 590 million to UNFPA.

chunks.title: Norway: national context
chunks.text: Co-founded CEPI, the vaccine research coalition, and co-chaired the Lusaka Agenda with Kenya.

chunks.title: Norway: national context
chunks.text: Sits on the WHO Executive Board.

chunks.title: Norway: national context
chunks.text: In PABS, opposes mandatory registration of users of genetic sequence databases and one-size-fits-all binding contracts. More than 100 civil society groups wrote to the Prime Minister objecting.

chunks.title: Norway: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Critics say Norway’s PABS stance enables ‘biopiracy’, and point out that Norwegian institutions themselves use the GISAID database, which requires registration.

chunks.title: Norway: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Presents itself as an equity champion while defending pharmaceutical industry incentives.

chunks.title: Norway: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): A country made rich by oil and gas, now trimming aid while expanding Norfund, its development investment fund.

chunks.title: Norway: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): The opposition Progress Party wants even deeper aid cuts.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: position on health financing
chunks.text: The Russian Federation opposes the ‘politicisation’ of WHO, rejects any supranational authority over sovereign health decisions, attacks Western hypocrisy over abandoned aid and sanctions, and offers itself to Africa as an alternative partner in outbreak response. Objectives: Stop WHO from being used to condemn Russia over Ukraine, which it calls ‘politicisation’ of a technical health body.; Get language recognising that unilateral sanctions harm access to medicines and medical equipment, and seek exemptions.; Expand bilateral health influence in Africa (laboratories, test kits, training) as an alternative to Western aid.; Keep strong sovereignty language in the Pandemic Agreement, IHR and PABS annex, and resist any outside oversight.; Remove ‘gender’, sexual orientation and comprehensive sexuality education language from health texts, in favour of ‘traditional family values’.. Red lines: Any text attributing attacks on health care to Russia or calling for accountability mechanisms.; Any binding compliance, inspection or verification powers for WHO.; ‘Gender-responsive’, sexual orientation and gender identity, or comprehensive sexuality education language.; Institutional penalties against Russia within WHO, such as relocating the European office or suspending its rights.; Endorsing Western-led sanctions or treating them as legitimate..

chunks.title: Russian Federation: national context
chunks.text: WHA79 adopted resolution WHA79/11 on the health impact of Russia’s war in Ukraine by 62 votes to 9, with 37 abstentions. Russia voted against.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: national context
chunks.text: WHO has verified more than 3,100 attacks on health care in Ukraine since the 2022 full-scale invasion, with attacks rising about 20% in 2025. WHO does not attribute each attack, but most occur in Russian strikes on Ukrainian territory.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: national context
chunks.text: Abstained on adopting the WHO Pandemic Agreement in May 2025, citing sovereignty.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: national context
chunks.text: Sent over 7,000 Bundibugyo Ebola test kits to Africa in June 2026, deployed a team to Uganda and supplied mobile labs to Uganda, Congo-Brazzaville and Ethiopia through its public health agency Rospotrebnadzor.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: national context
chunks.text: Has repeatedly tried to delete ‘gender’ and even the word ‘sexual’ from ‘sexual and reproductive health’ in WHO resolutions.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: national context
chunks.text: In 2022 WHO members voted to consider moving WHO’s European regional office functions out of Moscow.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Condemns Western ‘hypocrisy’ over aid cuts while its own contributions to WHO are modest, and documented strikes on Ukrainian hospitals continue.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): The sanctions argument contains some truth: banks and shipping firms ‘over-comply’ and disrupt medical supplies, even though food and medicine are formally exempt in most sanctions regimes.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its health diplomacy in Africa comes alongside security deals involving the Africa Corps (formerly Wagner), which critics see as buying influence and access to resources.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its Sputnik V COVID vaccine never received WHO emergency use listing.

chunks.title: Russian Federation: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Claims to defend WHO’s technical mandate while using procedural tactics (amendments, recorded votes) to block texts it dislikes.

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: position on health financing
chunks.text: Saudi Arabia presents itself as a generous humanitarian donor and a model of health transformation under Vision 2030, while insisting on its sovereign right to protect the Hajj with strict border measures and defending religious and cultural values against gender and sexual rights language. Objectives: Recognition of mass-gathering health security (Hajj and Umrah) as a global public good, and of the sovereign right to impose entry restrictions.; Showcase Vision 2030 reforms: digital health, supply-chain and logistics hubs, and Riyadh as a regional health centre.; Keep humanitarian health aid earmarked and visible (Yemen, Sudan, Syria, Gaza) rather than giving unearmarked core funding.; Add ‘in accordance with national laws, religious and cultural values’ caveats to any reproductive or sexual health text.; Strong language on the collapse of Gaza’s health system and attacks on health care in Palestine.. Red lines: No language on sexual orientation and gender identity, no ‘gender’ (prefers ‘women and girls’), no comprehensive sexuality education, nothing implying a right to abortion.; No binding limits on travel or entry measures during outbreaks, especially those affecting Hajj security.; Will not be pressured into large unearmarked pledges to WHO.; No texts that weaken language on Gaza or Palestinian health..

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: national context
chunks.text: Under Vision 2030, health services are moving from the ministry to a state-owned Health Holding Company and about 20 regional ‘health clusters’, with plans to raise the private sector’s share of health care from 40% to 65%.

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: national context
chunks.text: On 25 June 2026 it suspended all visas, including for the Umrah pilgrimage, for travellers from the DRC, Uganda and South Sudan because of Ebola, and banned its citizens from travelling there. WHO advises against travel bans.

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: national context
chunks.text: Hosts the Hajj, one of the world’s largest mass gatherings, and requires meningitis, polio, yellow fever and COVID-19 vaccinations from pilgrims.

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: national context
chunks.text: Gives health aid mainly through its own agency KSrelief, earmarked for specific crises (for example US$19.4 million to WHO for Yemen, Sudan and Syria in 2024), rather than flexible core funding. No major new WHO pledge after the US exit was found.

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: national context
chunks.text: Co-sponsored with Egypt, Nigeria and Russia a failed 2024 amendment to delete ‘gender-responsive’ from a WHA resolution, and led objections to ‘sexual orientation’ in WHO’s HIV strategy in 2022.

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Very wealthy but gives targeted, branded aid rather than core funding to WHO, which keeps control and soft-power benefits for Riyadh.

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its Ebola visa ban hit African Muslim pilgrims and contradicts WHO guidance that Saudi Arabia formally accepts under the IHR.

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Privatisation under Vision 2030 sits uneasily with its universal health coverage rhetoric. Migrant workers’ access to health care is a recurring criticism.

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its role in the Saudi-led coalition’s war in Yemen, which devastated Yemen’s health system and contributed to a massive cholera epidemic, undermines its image as a humanitarian health donor.

chunks.title: Saudi Arabia: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Balances between the absent US and an ascendant China. Its health minister met Chinese officials at WHA78.

chunks.title: South Africa: position on health financing
chunks.text: South Africa insists that ‘charity is not equity’: it demands binding benefit-sharing, African manufacturing and health sovereignty, and refuses to let the world’s largest HIV epidemic become collateral damage of donor politics. Objectives: PABS: binding contracts at the moment pathogens are accessed, with traceability, transparency, registration of users and national oversight of WHO network labs.; Benefit-sharing that works before the next crisis starts, not after patented products already exist.; African self-reliance: local manufacturing, a stronger Africa CDC and the African Medicines Agency.; Protect HIV and TB programmes through Global Fund replenishment and debt relief that gives countries room to spend on health.; Promote its National Health Insurance (NHI) plan as a model of universal health coverage.. Red lines: ‘Charity is not equity’: no benefit-sharing that is voluntary only.; No PABS that allows anonymous access to genetic sequence data.; No acceptance of US framing of South Africa or US-imposed conditions on aid.; No resolutions condemning Russia by name.; No travel bans against African countries during outbreaks, which it considers discriminatory and contrary to WHO advice..

chunks.title: South Africa: national context
chunks.text: Has the world’s largest HIV epidemic. In June 2026 the US confirmed a phased withdrawal of PEPFAR from South Africa. PEPFAR had provided about US$8 billion over two decades, roughly 17% of the HIV budget. The 2026 budget added about R26 billion for HIV.

chunks.title: South Africa: national context
chunks.text: Held the G20 presidency in 2025. The US and Argentina blocked a G20 health ministers’ declaration, so only a Chair’s Statement was issued. The US boycotted the Johannesburg leaders’ summit, and President Trump said South Africa would not be invited to the 2026 G20 in Miami.

chunks.title: South Africa: national context
chunks.text: Relations with the US are poor, including over South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice and US claims of persecution of white Afrikaners.

chunks.title: South Africa: national context
chunks.text: Spoke on behalf of the Africa Region on PABS at WHA79.

chunks.title: South Africa: national context
chunks.text: Pledged US$5 million to the Bundibugyo Ebola response.

chunks.title: South Africa: national context
chunks.text: Hosts Africa’s leading vaccine manufacturing ambitions, including Biovac and the WHO-backed mRNA technology hub at Afrigen.

chunks.title: South Africa: national context
chunks.text: Abstained on WHA79/11, the resolution on the health impact of Russia’s war in Ukraine.

chunks.title: South Africa: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Minister Motsoaledi insisted the PEPFAR exit ‘would not collapse’ the HIV programme, while NGOs report clinic closures and job losses. Critics call this denial.

chunks.title: South Africa: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): The NHI plan is contested within the governing coalition itself (the Democratic Alliance opposes parts of it) and faces court challenges, so its global showcase is fragile at home.

chunks.title: South Africa: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Non-aligned on Ukraine and close to Russia and China in BRICS, which draws Western accusations of selective concern for human rights and international law.

chunks.title: South Africa: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Pushes benefit-sharing for poorer countries while also hosting Africa’s main vaccine manufacturing ambitions, so it has commercial interests too.

chunks.title: South Africa: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Public health system suffers from mismanagement and corruption scandals, which weakens its claims about domestic capacity.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: position on health financing
chunks.text: The United Kingdom calls WHO ‘indispensable’ and champions science, antimicrobial resistance and reproductive rights, while it has cut aid to its lowest level in decades and keeps recruiting nurses from countries that cannot spare them. Objectives: An impartial, technically strong WHO that remains ‘indispensable’.; An ‘effective and equitable’ PABS annex that protects UK life sciences.; Leadership on antimicrobial resistance and tobacco and vaping control.; Protection of health facilities and workers in conflicts (Ukraine, Gaza, Sudan).; Defend sexual and reproductive health and rights and gender language against the US-led Geneva Consensus.. Red lines: No commitments implying a quick return to 0.7% aid spending.; No weakening of intellectual property protections for UK life sciences.; No retreat on sexual and reproductive health and gender language.; No restrictions on international recruitment beyond the voluntary WHO Code..

chunks.title: United Kingdom: national context
chunks.text: In February 2025 the Starmer government cut aid from 0.5% to 0.3% of national income by 2027 ‘to fully fund defence’ — about £9.2 billion in 2027, down from £15.3 billion in 2023. Excluding refugee costs spent inside the UK, real aid is around 0.2%.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: national context
chunks.text: Pledged £1.25 billion to Gavi for 2026–30 and £850 million to the Global Fund for 2026–28 (down 15%). Bilateral aid to several African countries has been almost eliminated.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: national context
chunks.text: Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July 2026 after a Labour leadership challenge. Labour backbenchers are pressing him to restore aid, but there is no commitment yet.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: national context
chunks.text: Nigeria and Ghana — both on WHO’s ‘red list’ of countries with critical health-worker shortages — were the UK’s second and third largest sources of new nurses in 2025–26.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: national context
chunks.text: Hosts 66 WHO Collaborating Centres and is a leader on antimicrobial resistance and tobacco control.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: national context
chunks.text: Supports Taiwan’s meaningful participation in WHO.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Still recruits nurses from red-list countries; the Royal College of Nursing calls it ‘unethical’.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Overseas nurse recruitment has halved since 2023–24, but mainly because of domestic migration politics and pressure from Reform UK, not ethics.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Counts money spent on asylum seekers in the UK as ‘aid’.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Labour’s manifesto promised ‘greater multilateral action’, but the share of aid going to multilateral bodies has not risen.

chunks.title: United Kingdom: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Cut aid to the poorest countries while increasing defence spending.

chunks.title: United States: position on health financing
chunks.text: The United States supports effective international health cooperation through transparent, results-driven partnerships that strengthen disease prevention while protecting national sovereignty and ensuring accountability for public spending. Objectives: Accountable and transparent international health funding with measurable outcomes, and a shift of partner countries to ‘self-reliance’ instead of permanent aid.; Stronger national preparedness against infectious diseases: ‘stop outbreaks before they reach our shores’, including fast access to pathogen samples and data.; Practical partnerships that deliver results: bilateral cooperation, medical research, disease surveillance and targeted assistance to vulnerable populations, including through faith-based health providers.; Hold WHO ‘accountable’ for its COVID-19 failures, bureaucracy and alleged deference to China, and encourage others to question its value.; Promote the Geneva Consensus agenda: protect ‘life’ and the family, and remove abortion and ‘gender ideology’ from global health texts.. Red lines: Prioritises national sovereignty, financial accountability and the responsible use of taxpayer funds; opposes arrangements that impose disproportionate financial obligations or lack oversight.; No obligations under WHO, the Pandemic Agreement or the amended IHR, and no text that ‘overlooks national policy boundaries’.; No sexual and reproductive health rights, abortion or gender language.; No multilateral benefit-sharing system (PABS) that would constrain US companies or US bilateral pathogen-access deals.; No funding to organisations that fail its ‘Promoting Human Flourishing’ conditions..

chunks.title: United States: national context
chunks.text: Withdrew from WHO (effective Jan 2026), leaving about US$260–280 million in unpaid dues. Formally rejected the 2024 IHR amendments in July 2025, and voted against the UN General Assembly’s political declaration on pandemics on 12 Oct 2026 (adopted 153–3–2).

chunks.title: United States: national context
chunks.text: Runs the ‘America First Global Health Strategy’ (Sept 2025): time-limited bilateral deals (MOUs) in which the US initially pays for frontline commodities and health workers, then partners must co-finance more each year. 36 MOUs signed by Oct 2026, including with the DRC, Nigeria and Kenya.

chunks.title: United States: national context
chunks.text: Congress appropriated US$9.42 billion for global health in FY2026, down from US$12.4 billion. PEPFAR survives under the State Department.

chunks.title: United States: national context
chunks.text: Pledged money for the Bundibugyo Ebola response (reported US commitments total about US$886 million including later pledges) and US$50 million to CEPI (confirmed by CEPI).

chunks.title: United States: national context
chunks.text: In August 2026 the US became the secretariat of the Geneva Consensus Declaration, an anti-abortion, ‘pro-family’ coalition of about 40 countries. Expanded Mexico City Policy rules (Feb 2026) bar US aid to organisations, including multilateral ones, involved in abortion, ‘gender ideology’ or DEI.

chunks.title: United States: national context
chunks.text: Draft US health MOUs sought pathogen samples and genetic sequence data within days, for up to 25 years, without guaranteed access to resulting vaccines. Kenya’s High Court suspended its deal over data-sharing concerns (later allowed to proceed on appeal), and Zambia removed the clause before signing.

chunks.title: United States: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Demands rapid pathogen access through bilateral deals while rejecting benefit-sharing multilaterally. Critics have called the draft MOU terms a ‘pathogen heist’.

chunks.title: United States: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Reporting linked a health package for Zambia to access to critical minerals, and MOU texts were posted and then taken down, undermining claims of transparency.

chunks.title: United States: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Champions ‘accountability’ while leaving unpaid WHO dues behind.

chunks.title: United States: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Its Ebola travel restrictions go against WHO advice, which the US no longer considers binding.

chunks.title: United States: team analysis
chunks.text: Team analysis (interpretation): Modelling published in The Lancet projects over 14 million additional deaths by 2030 if the USAID cuts continue; the administration disputes such estimates and says its new model is more efficient.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: US withdrawal from WHO
chunks.text: The US gave notice of withdrawal by Executive Order 14155 on 20 Jan 2025 and considers its exit effective 22 Jan 2026.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: US withdrawal from WHO
chunks.text: The US left roughly US$260–280 million in unpaid 2024–25 dues and said it would make no further payments. WHO's position is that withdrawal is not complete until arrears are paid, based on the 1948 US acceptance conditions.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: US withdrawal from WHO
chunks.text: WHA79 (May 2026) agreed by consensus to suspend US voting rights from WHA80 (May 2027) if about US$280 million in arrears remains unpaid. WHO still technically lists the US as a Member State in arrears; the US considers itself out.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: US withdrawal from WHO
chunks.text: Instead of WHO, the US runs the 'America First Global Health Strategy' (launched Sept 2025): bilateral health agreements (MOUs) with co-financing and transition-to-self-reliance requirements. 36 MOUs had been signed by 8 Oct 2026 (latest: Zambia, 5 years, US$2.49bn total with US$1.52bn from the US). The State Department says the MOUs total over US$27.2bn, including over US$16.1bn of US assistance.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Other withdrawals
chunks.text: Argentina gave notice of withdrawal on 17 Mar 2025 and says it left on 17 Mar 2026. WHO's Director-General said the notice should not be accepted as effective because the WHO Constitution has no withdrawal clause for Argentina. WHA79 'took note' of Argentina's communication and decided no further action was desirable, leaving its legal status ambiguous.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO finances
chunks.text: WHO's 2026–27 base programme budget is US$4.2 billion, 21% below the US$5.3 billion first proposed and roughly 15% below the 2024–25 base budget.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO finances
chunks.text: Before its withdrawal the US provided roughly a fifth of WHO's operational budget (CIDRAP; the share depends on the measure).

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO finances
chunks.text: WHA78 (May 2025) approved a further 20% increase in assessed (mandatory) contributions, about US$90 million a year.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO finances
chunks.text: China pledged US$500 million over five years at WHA78, making it WHO's largest state donor after the US exit.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO finances
chunks.text: In Feb 2026 WHO reported its base budget was about 85% funded. Estimates of the remaining gap have ranged from about US$1.06 billion to US$1.9 billion.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO finances
chunks.text: WHO is cutting roughly 22–25% of its staff (about 2,371 people by mid-2026), not counting thousands of consultants.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: The wider global health funding collapse
chunks.text: OECD preliminary data (Apr 2026): official development assistance from OECD donors fell 23.1% in real terms in 2025, to US$174.3 billion (0.26% of their combined national income), the largest one-year drop on record. US aid fell 56.9%, humanitarian aid 35.8%, and core funding to the UN 27%. A further 5.8% fall is forecast for 2026.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: The wider global health funding collapse
chunks.text: A Lancet modelling study (June 2025) projects more than 14 million additional deaths by 2030, including about 4.5 million children under five, if USAID cuts continue. This is a projection, not a count of deaths.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: The wider global health funding collapse
chunks.text: PEPFAR (the US HIV programme) now sits under the State Department and emphasises handing programmes over to national governments. HIV prevention medication (PrEP) has been largely restricted to pregnant and breastfeeding women, while the US backs rolling out the twice-yearly injection lenacapavir to up to 2 million people by 2028.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: The wider global health funding collapse
chunks.text: European donors are also cutting: the UK is reducing aid from 0.5% to 0.3% of national income by 2027; France and Germany have cut development budgets (exact figures vary by source).

chunks.title: Fact sheet: The wider global health funding collapse
chunks.text: Gavi's June 2025 replenishment raised over US$9 billion against an US$11.9 billion target for 2026–30; the US did not pledge.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: The wider global health funding collapse
chunks.text: The Global Fund's 8th replenishment (Nov 2025) raised about US$11.3 billion against an US$18 billion target. The US pledged US$4.6 billion (down from US$6 billion); Germany and the UK also pledged less.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: The wider global health funding collapse
chunks.text: The Accra Reset (Ghana, 2025) states that external health financing for Africa fell by almost 70% between 2021 and 2025.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO Pandemic Agreement and the IHR
chunks.text: The WHO Pandemic Agreement was adopted at WHA78 on 20 May 2025, after a committee vote of 124 in favour, 0 against and 11 abstentions (including Russia, Italy, Israel, the Netherlands, Poland and Iran).

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO Pandemic Agreement and the IHR
chunks.text: Under Article 12, manufacturers in the pathogen-sharing system would make 20% of real-time pandemic production available to WHO: at least 10% donated and the rest at affordable prices.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO Pandemic Agreement and the IHR
chunks.text: The PABS annex (Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing: rules for sharing virus samples and the benefits of products made from them) was NOT agreed by WHA79. Its deadline was extended to WHA80 (May 2027) or a special session. Negotiating rounds in July and September 2026 produced no agreement as of mid-October 2026.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO Pandemic Agreement and the IHR
chunks.text: Because the PABS annex is unfinished, the Pandemic Agreement cannot open for signature. It needs 60 ratifications to enter into force; it currently has none.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO Pandemic Agreement and the IHR
chunks.text: Main dividing line in PABS talks: the Africa Group and the 'Group for Equity' demand legally binding contracts, guaranteed affordable access and technology transfer; European and other developed countries prefer voluntary terms. Treatment of genetic sequence data is also disputed.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO Pandemic Agreement and the IHR
chunks.text: The 2024 amendments to the International Health Regulations (IHR), including a new 'pandemic emergency' alert level, entered into force on 19 Sep 2025. The US, Italy, Israel and Argentina rejected them.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO Pandemic Agreement and the IHR
chunks.text: On 12 Oct 2026 the UN General Assembly adopted a political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response by 153 votes to 3 (United States, Israel, Argentina), with 2 abstentions (New Zealand, Paraguay).

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHA79 (Geneva, 18–23 May 2026)
chunks.text: Theme: 'Reshaping global health: a shared responsibility'. Outcomes included a member-state-led process to reform the global health architecture, a strategy on the economics of health for all (2026–2030), the first update in 16 years to the WHO Code of Practice on international recruitment of health personnel, and a Global Action Plan on antimicrobial resistance 2026–2036.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHA79 (Geneva, 18–23 May 2026)
chunks.text: WHA79 heard that there had been 1,947 attacks on health care in the occupied Palestinian territory since Oct 2023, with Gaza health-sector losses estimated at US$6.78 billion.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: WHO leadership race
chunks.text: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus’s second term as Director-General ends in 2027. Candidates for the next Director-General include Indonesia’s Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin, Hans Kluge (Belgium, WHO Europe director), Hanan Balkhy (Saudi Arabia) and Hanan Al-Kuwari (Qatar). The Executive Board shortlists in January 2027 and the Assembly elects in May 2027.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, DRC (2026)
chunks.text: The outbreak was declared on 15 May 2026 in Ituri province, DRC. WHO declared it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) on 17 May 2026, but not a 'pandemic emergency'.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, DRC (2026)
chunks.text: As of mid-October 2026 there were roughly 9,000 confirmed cases and about 4,400 confirmed deaths (case fatality rate about 48%). WHO reported 8,728 cases and 4,205 deaths on 6 Oct; the US CDC reported 9,235 cases and 4,444 deaths on 15 Oct.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, DRC (2026)
chunks.text: The outbreak has spread to seven DRC provinces (Ituri is the epicentre; North Kivu has the highest fatality rate, about 60%). Uganda had imported cases but declared its outbreak over on 2 Sep 2026. Kenya confirmed an imported case on 6 Oct 2026, with no local spread reported. WHO rates the risk to neighbouring countries as high.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, DRC (2026)
chunks.text: It is by far the largest Bundibugyo outbreak ever (previous: Uganda 2007, about 131 cases; DRC 2012, about 60 cases), the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC, and the second-largest Ebola outbreak of any type after West Africa 2014–16. It is not the deadliest ever.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, DRC (2026)
chunks.text: There is no licensed vaccine or approved treatment for the Bundibugyo strain. The DRC began vaccinating front-line health workers with Ervebo (licensed for the Zaire strain, tested for cross-protection) on 28 Aug 2026. A CEPI-backed ring-vaccination trial ('Tumaini') and a Phase 1 trial of an Oxford/Serum Institute of India vaccine are under way.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, DRC (2026)
chunks.text: Response plans: a joint Africa CDC–WHO continental plan asks for US$518 million (Jun–Nov 2026); the DRC's updated 180-day plan asks for US$1.3 billion (separate plans, do not add together). The Pandemic Fund committed US$220.6 million. WHO reports critical funding gaps.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Other current health emergencies
chunks.text: Mpox: WHO ended its PHEIC in Sept 2025 and Africa CDC lifted its continental emergency in Jan 2026. The DRC declared its outbreak over in Apr 2026.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Other current health emergencies
chunks.text: Measles: Canada lost its measles elimination status in Nov 2025 after more than 5,000 cases, meaning the Americas region as a whole lost elimination status.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Other current health emergencies
chunks.text: Sudan: a new cholera outbreak since May 2026 had over 2,000 cases and 170 deaths by July, with fatality rates up to 13.7% in some areas. Sudan's 2026 humanitarian plan is about 40% funded.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Key concepts delegates use
chunks.text: Lusaka Agenda (2023, co-chaired by Kenya and Norway): align global health initiatives such as Gavi and the Global Fund behind country-led health systems, with integration and pooled procurement instead of separate disease-by-disease programmes.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Key concepts delegates use
chunks.text: Accra Reset / 'health sovereignty': launched by Ghana's President Mahama in 2025 in response to aid cuts. It calls for country-led compacts, more domestic financing and consolidating overlapping global health agencies (the consolidation idea is contested).

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Key concepts delegates use
chunks.text: Africa CDC promotes an Africa Health Sovereignty Initiative and domestic and innovative financing. The African Medicines Agency (Kigali) is the continent's regulator for locally manufactured medicines.

chunks.title: Fact sheet: Key concepts delegates use
chunks.text: Abuja Declaration (2001): African governments pledged to spend at least 15% of their budgets on health; few have met it. Debt-for-health swaps (e.g. the Global Fund's Debt2Health) convert debt repayments into health spending.

chunks.title: Strengthening health systems and outbreak preparedness amid declining global health funding
chunks.text: Access to health care and well-being is a universal issue, but how the problem shows up depends on each country’s wealth. The hardest hit are people in low-income countries that lack hospitals, doctors and money.

chunks.title: Strengthening health systems and outbreak preparedness amid declining global health funding
chunks.text: In 2025 global development aid fell by 23% — the largest drop on record. The United States, which provided 15–18% of WHO’s funding, withdrew from WHO in January 2026 and replaced most multilateral health aid with bilateral deals that require partner countries to pay more themselves. WHO has cut its budget by about a fifth and is laying off roughly a quarter of its staff.

chunks.title: Strengthening health systems and outbreak preparedness amid declining global health funding
chunks.text: Countries disagree sharply on what should replace the lost money. Some want richer countries to restore aid; others want poorer countries to fund their own health systems (‘health sovereignty’); others want new sources such as development banks, debt relief or health taxes.

chunks.title: Strengthening health systems and outbreak preparedness amid declining global health funding
chunks.text: Meanwhile the WHO Pandemic Agreement, adopted in May 2025, cannot take effect until countries agree on its PABS annex: the rules for sharing virus samples and the benefits (vaccines, medicines, money) that come from them. Developing countries want binding guarantees; most rich countries and pharmaceutical-producing states want voluntary terms.

chunks.title: Strengthening health systems and outbreak preparedness amid declining global health funding
chunks.text: The Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the DRC, declared a global health emergency in May 2026, shows what is at stake: there is no licensed vaccine, response plans are badly underfunded, and the outbreak has reached neighbouring countries.

chunks.title: Co-managing the double burden: strategies for simultaneously tackling infectious and non-communicable diseases (scoping review)
chunks.source: Infectious Diseases of Poverty 15:85 (2026), Li et al.
chunks.text: A scoping review of 41 systematic reviews/meta-analyses (2000–April 2026) finds two-way links between infectious and non-communicable diseases: infections such as hepatitis B/C, HPV and H. pylori raise specific cancer risks, tuberculosis is linked to chronic lung disease, and diabetes or heart disease worsen outcomes of TB, influenza and COVID-19. It argues for integrated prevention and care instead of separate programmes. Limits: Review of reviews; associations, not costed policy options; no country position.

chunks.title: The Impact of Economic Crises on Communicable Disease Transmission and Control: A Systematic Review
chunks.source: PLoS ONE 6(6): e20724 (2011), Suhrcke et al.
chunks.text: Of 37 studies included, 30 found worse infectious-disease outcomes during recessions (more contact in poorer living conditions, worse access to and retention in treatment). Migrants, homeless people and prisoners were especially exposed. The size of the effect depended strongly on how governments budgeted for health during the crisis. Limits: Mostly pre-2011 high-income settings; observational studies; old evidence.

chunks.title: The Contribution of International Agencies to the Control of Communicable Diseases
chunks.source: Archives of Medical Research 36 (2005) 731–738, Lazcano-Ponce et al.
chunks.text: A review describing how international agencies (WHO and others) have supported communicable-disease control and how unequal North–South investment in health research and capacity shapes global health inequality. Limits: 2005 narrative review; predates current WHO funding crisis.

chunks.title: Exploring the potential of mRNA vaccines in combatting communicable and non-communicable diseases in low-income and lower-middle-income countries
chunks.source: Annals of Medicine & Surgery (review), Paison et al.
chunks.text: A literature review: low- and lower-middle-income countries face a double burden of infectious and non-communicable diseases (WHO projects NCDs at 70% of deaths there by 2050). mRNA platforms are fast and adaptable, but cold-chain storage, stability and delivery logistics limit their use in resource-poor settings without targeted investment. Limits: Narrative review; potential, not demonstrated programme results.

chunks.title: High prevalence of infectious diseases and drug-resistant microorganisms in asylum seekers admitted to hospital
chunks.source: PLoS ONE 11(5): e0154791 (2016), Ravensbergen et al.
chunks.text: In 273 asylum seekers seen at a Dutch university hospital, 48% had an infectious disease (mainly malaria or tuberculosis) and 31% carried multi-drug-resistant organisms; screening and infection control on arrival matter. Limits: Single hospital, hospital-admitted patients only (not all asylum seekers).

chunks.title: Surveillance on speed: syndromic surveillance of infectious diseases in migrants' mass accommodations, Germany 2016–2017
chunks.source: Eurosurveillance 23(40) (2018), Sarma et al. (Robert Koch Institute)
chunks.text: The Robert Koch Institute describes a simple, flexible syndromic-surveillance toolkit used in German reception centres to detect outbreaks early among newly arrived migrants. Limits: Describes a tool and its field use; German national context, not a policy position.

chunks.title: Digital Inclusion among Community Older Adults in the Republic of Korea: Measuring Digital Skills and Health Consequences
chunks.source: European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education (2024), Pan, Aung, Nam et al.
chunks.text: A survey of 434 adults aged 65+ in two Korean cities (plus focus groups): 80.65% had never used the internet or digital technology to access health care and 85.45% never for care services for older persons, even in a highly digital country; digital social skills were positively associated with self-rated health. Limits: Two cities, recruited through welfare centres — limited generalisability. A research finding, not Korean government policy.

chunks.title: Australia: student stance
chunks.location: Agenda A. Breaking the Deadlock on a Global Plastics Treaty · Australia
chunks.text: Australia supports a legally binding global plastics treaty addressing plastic pollution throughout its lifecycle while emphasizing effective implementation, marine protection, and fair financial and technical support for developing countries. Wants: Establish a legally binding global plastics treaty covering the entire plastics lifecycle, including production, design, consumption, and waste management.; Reduce plastic pollution in oceans and protect marine ecosystems.; Improve global recycling systems and support developing countries with financial and technical assistance.. Limits: Ensure that treaty obligations are practical and internationally coordinated.; Protect industries and workers through a realistic transition toward sustainable materials.; Ensure that developing countries receive sufficient resources to implement treaty commitments..

chunks.title: Brazil: student stance
chunks.location: Agenda A. Breaking the Deadlock on a Global Plastics Treaty · Brazil
chunks.text: Brazil supports international cooperation to reduce plastic pollution and expand circular-economy systems while protecting national policy flexibility and ensuring that developing countries receive adequate implementation support. Wants: Establish a global framework addressing plastic pollution while allowing countries flexibility in implementation.; Improve waste collection, recycling, and circular-economy infrastructure.; Provide financial and technological support to developing countries.. Limits: Protect national development priorities and policy autonomy.; Avoid imposing identical obligations on countries with different economic capacities.; Ensure that restrictions on plastics do not create unfair burdens for domestic industries and workers..

chunks.title: Brazil in the negotiation record (ENB)
chunks.text: In response to a request for clarification by BRAZIL, INC Chair Vayas confirmed that neither the Chair's Draft Text Proposal... would be annexed [Page 8] — Only procedural and facilitation roles are recorded (co-chaired Contact Group 1; co-facilitated informals on several articles and on health [Pages 4-5, 7]). In INC-5.3 Brazil supported Kuwait's (oil-producer-aligned) call to suspend the session and seek a Chair by acclamation, which hints at consensus-leaning procedure but is not a substantive position.

chunks.title: Chile: student stance
chunks.location: Agenda A. Breaking the Deadlock on a Global Plastics Treaty · Chile
chunks.text: Chile supports ambitious and legally binding international action against plastic pollution while emphasizing clear global standards, effective waste management, and equitable implementation. Wants: Negotiate a binding treaty with clear global rules for reducing plastic pollution.; Strengthen restrictions on problematic plastics and improve product design.; Support coastal communities and developing countries in managing plastic waste.. Limits: Ensure that treaty obligations are achievable and supported by adequate financing.; Avoid fragmented regulations that make international trade and compliance unnecessarily difficult.; Protect industries and communities that depend on affordable materials..

chunks.title: China: student stance
chunks.location: Agenda A. Breaking the Deadlock on a Global Plastics Treaty · China
chunks.text: China supports a cooperative global response to plastic pollution focused on waste management, recycling, and technological innovation while emphasizing national circumstances, development rights, and balanced treaty obligations. Wants: Strengthen international cooperation on plastic waste management, recycling, and environmentally friendly production.; Improve technology transfer and financing for developing countries.; Develop treaty obligations that account for national circumstances and different levels of development.. Limits: Preserve national sovereignty over industrial and environmental policy.; Oppose inflexible obligations that impose disproportionate costs on developing economies.; Ensure that restrictions on plastic production do not unfairly disadvantage domestic manufacturing and trade..

chunks.title: China in the negotiation record (ENB)
chunks.text: CHINA stressed that plastic pollution is far more complex than expected, with great disparity among economies in terms of plastic dependencies... and waste management capabilities. [Page 10] — China, speaking for itself, also backed the Chair's proposed way forward together with India [Page 8]. The text had no provisions on scope or sustainable production. ENB has no explicit Chinese statement on production caps.

chunks.title: Colombia: student stance
chunks.location: Agenda A. Breaking the Deadlock on a Global Plastics Treaty · Colombia
chunks.text: Colombia supports ambitious international action to prevent plastic pollution, strengthen producer responsibility, and improve waste management while protecting vulnerable communities and ensuring equitable implementation. Wants: Establish binding international measures to reduce plastic pollution and prevent plastics from entering rivers and oceans.; Improve producer responsibility and waste collection.; Provide funding and technology for countries with limited waste-management infrastructure.. Limits: Ensure that treaty obligations are accompanied by financial and technical assistance.; Protect vulnerable communities and informal waste workers.; Avoid shifting the costs of plastic pollution onto developing countries and consumers alone..

chunks.title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: student stance
chunks.location: Agenda A. Breaking the Deadlock on a Global Plastics Treaty · Democratic Republic of the Congo
chunks.text: The Democratic Republic of the Congo supports international efforts to reduce plastic pollution and improve waste management while insisting on financial assistance, technology transfer, and respect for developing countries' economic circumstances. Wants: Establish a global treaty that reduces plastic pollution and improves waste collection.; Provide funding for waste-management infrastructure and recycling systems.; Support public education and technology transfer to reduce environmental contamination.. Limits: Ensure that developing countries are not expected to implement expensive obligations without financial support.; Protect economic development and employment opportunities.; Avoid regulations that disproportionately burden countries with limited infrastructure..

chunks.title: Fiji: student stance
chunks.location: Agenda A. Breaking the Deadlock on a Global Plastics Treaty · Fiji
chunks.text: Fiji advocates an ambitious global plastics treaty that addresses pollution at its source while prioritizing marine protection and ensuring that small island developing states receive the resources needed to implement it. Wants: Adopt a strong treaty that reduces plastic pollution at its source.; Restrict problematic single-use plastics and improve controls over plastic waste entering the ocean.; Fund waste-management systems and marine conservation in small island developing states.. Limits: Climate-vulnerable developing countries should not be expected to manage displacement without adequate international financial and technical assistance.; Climate finance should be accessible, predictable, and based on the needs of vulnerable countries.; Relocation programs must protect human rights, livelihoods, cultural identity, and community ties.; Bangladesh should not be expected to accept unlimited responsibility for a crisis largely driven by global emissions..

chunks.title: Three approaches to deep-sea mining (class framework)
chunks.text: Deep-sea mining is not the same as land-based mining. States may agree on responsible sourcing on land but disagree sharply over whether commercial seabed mining should proceed. For your MUN debate, distinguish three positions: * Precautionary approach: Do not authorize commercial deep-sea mining until major scientific uncertainties and environmental risks are adequately addressed. * Conditional development: Permit mining only under strict environmental rules, monitoring, and enforceable liability. * Resource-development approach: Support mineral extraction to meet energy-transition needs, provided that environmental standards and international governance are established. The International Seabed Authority (ISA) is central to negotiations over mineral activities in the international seabed area. For land-based critical minerals, national governments and relevant supply-chain initiatives are more directly involved.
